What is Lua: Lua is a lightweight, high-level, dynamically typed scripting language designed for embedded use in applications. Created in 1993 at PUC-Rio in Brazil, it's widely used in game development (World of Warcraft, Roblox), embedded systems, and configuration scripting. Common mistake: confusing Lua's simplicity with lack of power — Lua's metatables and first-class functions enable sophisticated programming patterns. Best practice: use local variables by default, avoid global pollution, and leverage Lua's table-as-structure paradigm.

-- Lua is dynamically typed — no type declarations
print("Hello from Lua 5.4!")

-- Lua is lightweight and fast
-- Primarily used for embedded scripting

-- Check your Lua version
print(_VERSION)  -- Lua 5.4
Lua Syntax: Lua uses keywords instead of curly braces for blocks, and whitespace is not significant (unlike Python). Statements can end with semicolons but they're optional. Blocks are delimited with keywords like then/end, do/end, and function/end. Common mistake: forgetting the 'then' keyword after if/elseif conditions. Best practice: use semicolons only to separate statements on the same line; omit them otherwise for cleaner code.

-- Keywords delimit blocks, not braces or indentation
if true then
    print("Inside if block")
end

-- Semicolons are optional
x = 10; y = 20  -- two statements on one line

-- No whitespace significance
if true then
print("No indentation needed")  -- valid, but ugly
end

-- Multiple statements per line
name = "Lua"; print("Hello, " .. name)
Comments: Lua supports single-line comments with -- and multi-line comments with --[[ ]]. Multi-line comments can be nested with additional brackets. Common mistake: forgetting that --[[ ]] comments cannot contain the sequence ']]' unless you use an equal sign format. Best practice: use --[[ ]] for commenting out blocks of code during debugging, and -- for explanatory comments.

-- This is a single-line comment

--[[ This is a multi-line comment
     spanning multiple lines
]]

--[[[ This is a nested comment --[[ inner ]] --]]]

print("Comments don't affect execution")

--[[ Debug: temporarily disable code
print("This won't run")
print("Neither will this")
--]]
Hello World: The print() function outputs text to stdout with a trailing newline. Multiple arguments are separated by tabs. Common mistake: forgetting that print adds a tab between arguments — use io.write() for exact output control. Best practice: use print() for quick debugging and io.write() for formatted output where you need precise control.

print("Hello, World!")  -- basic output

print("Hello", "World")   -- prints: Hello\tWorld

-- Multiple arguments with different types
print("The answer is", 42)

-- String concatenation alternative
print("Hello" .. " " .. "World")
Interactive Mode: Lua's REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) lets you execute code interactively by running 'lua' with no arguments. Use dofile() to load and execute a Lua file, and loadfile() to compile without running. Common mistake: expecting the REPL to persist local variables between input lines — each line is a separate chunk. Best practice: use dofile() during development to reload modules without restarting the REPL.

-- dofile() loads and runs a Lua file
-- dofile("myprogram.lua")

-- loadfile() compiles but doesn't run
-- local f = loadfile("mymodule.lua")
-- f()  -- now execute it

-- In REPL, you can evaluate expressions directly
print("REPL basics: Lua 5.4")

-- load() compiles a string
local f = load("return 2 + 2")
print(f())  -- 4
Lua Versions & Compatibility: Lua versions: 5.1 (most compatible, used by LuaJIT, World of Warcraft), 5.2 (environments changed), 5.3 (integers, bit32), 5.4 (generational GC, const/close, to-be-closed vars). LuaJIT is a JIT-compiled implementation compatible with Lua 5.1. Luau is Roblox's variant with typed Lua. Check _VERSION to detect version at runtime.

print(_VERSION)  -- "Lua 5.4"

if _VERSION == "Lua 5.1" then
    print("Running Lua 5.1 (or LuaJIT)")
elseif _VERSION == "Lua 5.4" then
    print("Lua 5.4 features available")
end

-- Lua 5.3+: integer division
local result = 10 // 3  -- 3 (floor division, 5.3+)

-- Lua 5.4: const variables
local const x = 42  -- cannot reassign (5.4+)

-- Lua 5.2+: goto
::loop::
print("Lua 5.2+ goto")
-- Lua 5.4: to-be-closed variables
-- local f <close> = io.open("file.txt")

Dynamic Typing: Lua is dynamically typed — variables don't have types; values do. A variable can hold any type of value at any time. There's no variable declaration keyword (unlike 'let' or 'var'); assigning a value creates the variable globally unless 'local' is used. Common mistake: forgetting 'local' creates a global variable, even inside loops and functions. Best practice: always use local for variables that should be scoped to the current block.

x = 42          -- x is now a number
x = "hello"     -- x is now a string (no error)

-- Local vs global
local y = 10     -- local scope
z = 20           -- global scope

print(type(x))   -- string
print(type(y))   -- number

-- Variables default to nil before assignment
local a
print(a)         -- nil
nil: nil is Lua's "no value" type, representing the absence of a value. Global variables default to nil, table keys with no value are nil, and assigning nil to a table key removes it from the table. Common mistake: treating nil as false in comparisons — nil is falsy, but is not the same as false. Best practice: use x == nil to check for nil explicitly, not just if x then, since false is also falsy.

local a  -- not assigned, value is nil
print(a)   -- nil

-- nil removes table elements
t = {1, 2, 3}
t[2] = nil  -- removes the second element
print(t[2]) -- nil (gap in array)

-- nil is falsy but distinct from false
if nil then
    print("won't print")
else
    print("nil is falsy")
end

print(nil == false)  -- false (they are different)
boolean: Lua's boolean type has two values: true and false. Only nil and false are falsy; everything else (including 0 and empty string) is truthy. Common mistake: assuming 0 or empty string is falsy — they are not in Lua. Best practice: use explicit comparisons like x == nil for clarity instead of relying on truthiness.

local a = true
local b = false

-- Only nil and false are falsy
if 0 then print("0 is truthy in Lua") end
if "" then print("empty string is truthy") end

-- Boolean operators return values, not booleans
print(4 and 5)     -- 5 (last truthy)
print(nil or 5)    -- 5 (first truthy)

-- not always returns a boolean
print(not nil)     -- true
print(not 42)      -- false
number: All Lua numbers are double-precision floating-point by default. Lua 5.3+ also provides integers (64-bit) that are used internally when appropriate. Arithmetic operations automatically choose between integer and float representations. Common mistake: assuming integer division truncates — use // (floor division) for integer division. Best practice: be aware that large integers (> 2^53) lose precision due to double representation.

local n = 42         -- integer subtype
local f = 3.14       -- float

print(type(n))       -- number
print(type(f))       -- number

-- Conversion
print(tonumber("123"))  -- 123
print(tostring(3.14))   -- "3.14"

-- Math with integers
print(10 / 3)   -- 3.3333333333333 (float division)
print(10 // 3)  -- 3 (floor division, Lua 5.3+)
print(10 % 3)   -- 1 (modulo)
string: Strings in Lua are immutable byte sequences. You can use single quotes, double quotes, or long brackets [[ ]] for multi-line strings. Escape sequences work inside quoted strings (\n, \t, \", \'). Common mistake: using # on strings counts bytes, not characters — for UTF-8 strings, use utf8.len(). Best practice: use [[ ]] for strings containing quotes or line breaks to avoid escaping.

local s1 = 'single quotes'
local s2 = "double quotes"
local s3 = [[multi-line
string with [[nested]] brackets]]

print(#s1)            -- 13 (byte length)
print("hello" .. " " .. "world")  -- concatenation

-- Escape sequences
print("Line1\nLine2")   -- newline
print("Tab\there")       -- tab
print("Quote: \"hi\"")  -- double quote

-- Multi-line with brackets
local html = [[
<html>
<body>Hello</body>
</html>
]]
print(html)
type() and Coercion: The type() function returns a string describing the type of a value. Lua automatically coerces strings to numbers in arithmetic and numbers to strings in concatenation. Common mistake: relying on automatic coercion in comparisons — '10' == 10 is false (no coercion in equality). Best practice: use tonumber() and tostring() explicitly for clarity.

print(type(42))          -- number
print(type("hello"))     -- string
print(type(nil))          -- nil
print(type(true))         -- boolean
print(type({}))           -- table
print(type(print))        -- function

-- Automatic coercion
print(10 .. 20)    -- "1020" (numbers coerced to string)
print("10" + 20)   -- 30 (string coerced to number)

-- No coercion in equality
print("10" == 10)  -- false

-- Explicit conversion
print(tonumber("10") == 10)  -- true
Multiple Assignment: Lua supports simultaneous multiple assignment: `a, b = 1, 2`. Right-hand values are adjusted to match left-hand variables: extra values discarded, missing values become nil. Useful for swapping: `a, b = b, a`. Function calls can return multiple values captured by multiple assignment.

-- Basic multiple assignment
local a, b, c = 1, 2, 3
print(a, b, c)  -- 1    2    3

-- Swapping (no temp variable needed!)
local x, y = 10, 20
x, y = y, x
print(x, y)  -- 20    10

-- Value adjustment
local p, q, r = 1, 2  -- r = nil
local s, t = 1, 2, 3  -- t = 2 (3 discarded)

-- Multiple returns from functions
function minmax(a, b)
    if a < b then return a, b
    else return b, a end
end

local lo, hi = minmax(42, 17)
print(lo, hi)  -- 17    42

-- Collect extra returns with (...) varargs
function multi() return 1, 2, 3, 4 end
local first, second, rest = multi()
print(rest)  -- 3 (third return, 4 discarded)

Arithmetic: Lua provides standard arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, ^ (exponentiation), // (floor division, Lua 5.3+), and % (modulo). The modulo operator always takes the sign of the divisor. Common mistake: using / when you want integer division — use // (floor division) instead. Best practice: understand that % in Lua is defined as a % b == a - (a // b) * b, which differs from C's remainder.

print(10 + 3)   -- 13
print(10 - 3)   -- 7
print(10 * 3)   -- 30
print(10 / 3)   -- 3.3333333333333
print(10 // 3)  -- 3 (floor division)
print(10 % 3)   -- 1 (modulo)
print(2 ^ 10)   -- 1024.0 (exponentiation)

-- Modulo sign follows divisor
print(-10 % 3)  -- 2  (not -1 like in C)
print(10 % -3)  -- -2 (not 1 like in C)
Relational: Lua's relational operators are: == (equal), ~= (not equal), <, >, <=, >=. They always return a boolean. Tables and userdata are compared by reference, not by value. Common mistake: using == to compare tables — it checks reference equality, not structural equality. Best practice: implement custom comparison via metamethods if table equality is needed.

print(10 == 10)  -- true
print(10 ~= 5)   -- true (~= is not equal)
print(10 < 5)    -- false
print(10 >= 10)  -- true

-- Strings compare lexicographically
print("apple" < "banana")  -- true

-- Tables compare by reference
local a = {1, 2, 3}
local b = {1, 2, 3}
print(a == b)    -- false (different references)

-- Chained comparisons are NOT supported
-- print(1 < 2 < 3)  -- ERROR: cannot compare boolean with number
Logical: Lua's logical operators are: and, or, not. They use short-circuit evaluation: 'and' stops at the first falsy value; 'or' stops at the first truthy value. Common mistake: assuming logical operators always return booleans — they return one of their operands. Best practice: use the 'a or b' idiom for default values.

print(true and false)  -- false
print(false or 42)      -- 42 (returns operand, not boolean)
print(not "")           -- true

-- Short-circuit evaluation
local function risky()
    print("risky called!")
    return 42
end

print(false and risky())  -- false (risky NOT called)
print(true or risky())    -- true (risky NOT called)

-- Default value idiom
local function greet(name)
    name = name or "Guest"  -- default if nil
    print("Hello, " .. name)
end
greet()          -- Hello, Guest
greet("Lua")    -- Hello, Lua
Concatenation and Length: The .. operator concatenates strings (coercing numbers). The # operator returns the length of a string or array-like table. Common mistake: using # on tables with nil gaps — # returns an undefined result for non-sequence tables. Best practice: only use # on tables that are proper sequences (consecutive integer keys starting at 1, no nil values).

-- Concatenation
print("Hello" .. " " .. "World")  -- Hello World
print("Value: " .. 42)            -- Value: 42

-- Length operator on strings
print(#"hello")      -- 5

-- Length operator on array-like tables
local arr = {10, 20, 30, 40}
print(#arr)          -- 4

-- CAUTION: # on tables with gaps is undefined
local t = {1, 2, nil, 4}
print(#t)            -- 4 or 2 (implementation-dependent)
Operator Precedence: Lua's operator precedence (highest to lowest): ^, unary - not #, * / // %, + -, .., < > <= >= ~= ==, and, or. Exponentiation is right-associative; all others are left-associative. Common mistake: assuming bitwise operators exist — Lua 5.3+ has them in bit32 library, not as operators. Best practice: use parentheses generously for complex expressions.

-- Precedence examples
print(2 + 3 * 4)   -- 14 (multiplication first)
print((2 + 3) * 4) -- 20 (parentheses override)

-- Concatenation is lower than arithmetic
print("sum: " .. 2 + 3)  -- ERROR: cannot concat number
print("sum: " .. (2 + 3)) -- "sum: 5"

-- not binds tighter than and/or
print(not true and false) -- false (not true = false)
print(not (true and false)) -- true

if/elseif/else: Lua's if statement ends with 'end' and uses 'then' after conditions. Use 'elseif' (one word) for multiple branches. Conditions must be boolean or use truthiness. Common mistake: using 'else if' instead of 'elseif' — 'else if' requires a nested if/end block. Best practice: keep conditions simple; use local variables to store complex conditions.

local score = 85

if score >= 90 then
    print("A")
elseif score >= 80 then
    print("B")
elseif score >= 70 then
    print("C")
else
    print("F")
end

-- Nested if with multiple conditions
local x, y = 5, 10
if x > 0 then
    if y > 0 then
        print("Both positive")
    end
end
while: The while loop executes as long as the condition is true. The condition is checked before each iteration. Common mistake: forgetting to update the loop variable, causing infinite loops. Best practice: use while for loops with variable conditions and for loops when the iteration count is known.

local i = 1
while i <= 5 do
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
end

-- While with break
local x = 1
while true do
    if x > 3 then break end
    print("x = " .. x)
    x = x + 1
end
repeat/until: The repeat/until loop always executes its body at least once before checking the condition. This differs from while loops that may never execute. Common mistake: confusing repeat/until with while — the condition is checked AFTER the body. Best practice: use repeat/until when you need guaranteed at-least-once execution.

local i = 1
repeat
    print(i)
    i = i + 1
until i > 5

-- Always executes at least once
local x = 10
repeat
    print("Will print once")
until x > 20

-- Reading input until valid
repeat
    -- simulate user input
    local input = "yes"
    print("Continue? (yes/no)")
until input == "no"
Numeric for: The numeric for loop: for var = init, limit, step do end. The loop variable is local to the loop body. Step defaults to 1 if omitted. The limit is evaluated once before the loop starts. Common mistake: modifying the loop variable inside the body — it will be reset each iteration. Best practice: don't modify the loop variable; use a separate variable if needed.

for i = 1, 5 do
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1 2 3 4 5

-- With custom step
for i = 1, 10, 2 do
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1 3 5 7 9

-- Reverse loop
for i = 5, 1, -1 do
    print(i)
end
-- prints 5 4 3 2 1

-- Loop variable is local
print(i)  -- nil (variable not accessible outside)
Generic for: The generic for loop iterates over iterators like pairs(), ipairs(), and custom iterators. It uses the pattern: for var-list in iterator, state, initial-value do. Common mistake: using pairs() when you need ordered iteration — pairs() doesn't guarantee order. Best practice: use ipairs() for array-style tables and pairs() for dictionaries.

-- ipairs() for array-like tables (1-indexed, stops at nil)
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}
for i, v in ipairs(fruits) do
    print(i, v)
end

-- pairs() for all keys (unordered)
local info = {name = "Lua", year = 1993}
for k, v in pairs(info) do
    print(k, v)
end

-- Iterate string characters
for i, c in ipairs({"a", "b", "c"}) do
    print(c)
end
break: The break statement terminates the innermost enclosing loop (for, while, or repeat). Lua does NOT have continue — you must use conditional wrapping to skip iterations. Common mistake: trying to use 'continue' — it doesn't exist in Lua. Best practice: use if/else blocks to skip iterations instead of continue.

for i = 1, 10 do
    if i == 5 then break end
    print(i)
end
-- prints 1 2 3 4

-- Simulating continue with if
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i % 2 == 0 then  -- skip evens
        -- continue logic: skip to next iteration
        goto continue
    end
    print(i)
    ::continue::
end

-- Break in nested loops (only breaks innermost)
for i = 1, 3 do
    for j = 1, 3 do
        if j == 2 then break end
        print(i, j)
    end
end

Table Basics: Tables are Lua's sole data structuring mechanism, combining arrays, dictionaries, objects, and modules. They're created with {} and are dynamically resizable. Tables are reference types — assigning a table to another variable creates a reference, not a copy. Common mistake: assuming tables are 0-indexed — Lua arrays conventionally start at index 1. Best practice: always start array indices at 1 for compatibility with #, ipairs(), and table library functions.

-- Creating tables
local empty = {}
local t = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

-- Tables are reference types
local a = {1, 2, 3}
local b = a  -- b references the same table
b[1] = 99
print(a[1])  -- 99

-- Dynamic resizing
t[6] = 6   -- add element
t[1] = nil -- remove element (creates gap)

-- Mixed content
local mixed = {"hello", 42, true, {}}
print(mixed[1])  -- "hello"
Constructors: Table constructors create and initialize tables in a single expression. Use curly braces with comma-separated values. Common mistake: mixing key-value and array-style constructors can produce confusing results. Best practice: use array-style ({1, 2, 3}) for sequences and key-value style ({x=1, y=2}) for records.
Array-style Tables: Lua arrays are 1-indexed and can hold any value type. The # operator returns the length of a sequence. Array indices are conventional — Lua internally uses any value type as a key. Common mistake: assuming # gives the count of elements in a table with gaps — it doesn't. Best practice: maintain tables as proper sequences (no nil gaps) when using array operations.

-- 1-indexed arrays
local arr = {10, 20, 30, 40}
print(arr[1])     -- 10 (first element)
print(#arr)       -- 4 (length)

-- Adding elements
arr[#arr + 1] = 50  -- append
print(#arr)         -- 5

-- Nil gaps create undefined behavior
local gappy = {1, 2, nil, 4}
print(#gappy)      -- undefined (may be 4 or 2)

-- Traversing safely
for i = 1, #arr do
    print(arr[i])
end
Table Manipulation: The table library provides: table.insert(t, pos, val), table.remove(t, pos), table.sort(t, comp), and table.concat(t, sep). These modify the table in-place. Common mistake: table.insert with pos shifts all subsequent elements — O(n) operation. Best practice: use t[#t+1] = val for appending (faster than table.insert).

local t = {3, 1, 4, 1, 5}

-- Insert
table.insert(t, 9)       -- append: {3,1,4,1,5,9}
table.insert(t, 2, 99)   -- insert at position 2

-- Remove
local removed = table.remove(t)  -- pop last
table.remove(t, 2)               -- remove at position 2

-- Sort
table.sort(t)  -- ascending sort

-- Concat (strings only)
local words = {"hello", "world", "lua"}
print(table.concat(words, ", "))  -- "hello, world, lua"
Iterating Arrays: Use ipairs() for sequential iteration over array-style tables (stops at first nil). Use a numeric for loop for complete control. Common mistake: using pairs() for arrays — it doesn't guarantee order. Best practice: use ipairs() when you need ordered index-value pairs; use a numeric for loop when you need to modify elements during iteration.

local t = {"a", "b", "c", "d"}

-- ipairs() - ordered, stops at first nil
for i, v in ipairs(t) do
    print(i, v)
end

-- Numeric for - full control
for i = 1, #t do
    t[i] = t[i]:upper()  -- modify in place
end

-- Updating during iteration
for i = #t, 1, -1 do
    if t[i] == "B" then
        table.remove(t, i)
    end
end

Dictionary-style Tables: Tables can use any value (except nil) as a key. String keys can be set with dot notation (t.key) or bracket notation (t['key']). Bracket notation is required for non-string keys or keys with spaces. Common mistake: using t.key when key contains spaces or special characters — use t["key name"] instead. Best practice: prefer bracket notation for dynamic keys and dot notation for literal string keys.

-- String keys
local person = {
    name = "Alice",
    age = 30,
    ["favorite color"] = "blue"  -- space in key
}

print(person.name)              -- Alice (dot notation)
print(person["age"])            -- 30 (bracket notation)
print(person["favorite color"]) -- blue

-- Non-string keys
local weird = {}
weird[true] = "boolean key"
weird[42] = "number key"
weird[{[1]={}}] = "table key"  -- not recommended!

print(weird[true])  -- boolean key
Nested Tables: Tables can contain other tables as values, creating nested structures like multi-dimensional arrays, trees, and graphs. Access nested values by chaining brackets or dots. Common mistake: creating a shallow copy with = when you need a deep copy — = only copies the reference. Best practice: write a recursive copy function for deep copies of nested tables.
pairs() Iteration: pairs() iterates over all key-value pairs in a table, including array-style indices. The iteration order is NOT guaranteed. For ordered iteration, collect keys into a sorted array first. Common mistake: relying on pairs() to visit keys in insertion order — it doesn't. Best practice: use pairs() for dictionary-style tables and ipairs() or numeric for for arrays.

local config = {
    host = "localhost",
    port = 8080,
    debug = true,
    timeout = 30
}

-- Unordered iteration
for key, value in pairs(config) do
    print(key .. " = " .. tostring(value))
end

-- Sorted iteration (by key)
local keys = {}
for k in pairs(config) do
    table.insert(keys, k)
end
table.sort(keys)
for _, k in ipairs(keys) do
    print(k .. " = " .. tostring(config[k]))
end
Table Size Caveats: The # operator only works reliably for sequences (consecutive integer keys from 1 with no nil gaps). For dictionaries, use next() to count elements. Common mistake: using # on a dictionary — it returns 0 or an arbitrary value. Best practice: write a table.size() helper using next() for non-array tables.

-- # only works on sequences
local array = {10, 20, 30}
print(#array)  -- 3 (correct)

-- # on dictionary
local dict = {a = 1, b = 2, c = 3}
print(#dict)   -- 0 (wrong! dictionaries aren't sequences)

-- Counting elements with next()
local function table_size(t)
    local count = 0
    for _ in pairs(t) do
        count = count + 1
    end
    return count
end

print(table_size(dict))  -- 3 (correct)

-- next() iteration manually
local k = next(dict)
while k do
    print(k, dict[k])
    k = next(dict, k)
end
Table Constructors Mixed Forms: Lua allows mixing array-style and dictionary-style entries in a single constructor. Array items get integer keys starting at 1; dictionary items get string keys. Understanding how Lua assigns keys is crucial for predictable results. Common mistake: expecting array-style indices to skip over dictionary items — array indices are assigned based on position counting only array items.

-- Mixed constructor
local t = {
    "first",          -- [1] = "first"
    "second",         -- [2] = "second"
    key1 = "value1", -- ["key1"] = "value1"
    "third",          -- [3] = "third"
    key2 = "value2", -- ["key2"] = "value2"
}

print(t[1])     -- first
print(t[3])     -- third
print(t.key1)   -- value1
print(t.key2)   -- value2

-- Explicit key assignment
local explicit = {
    [1] = "one",
    ["name"] = "test",
    [2] = "two",
    [3] = "three"
}

-- Table constructors for sets
local set = {
    apple = true,
    banana = true,
    cherry = true
}
if set.apple then print("apple is in set") end
Table Manipulation Library: table library provides: table.insert, table.remove, table.sort, table.concat, table.pack, table.unpack, table.move. table.sort accepts comparator function. table.concat efficiently joins string arrays. table.pack creates array from varargs with .n field. table.unpack expands table into values. These work on array-like tables (consecutive integer keys starting at 1).

Function Definition: Functions are first-class values in Lua, created with the function keyword or as anonymous functions. The return keyword exits a function and optionally returns values. Common mistake: forgetting 'return' — functions without an explicit return return nil. Best practice: declare local functions for internal use and assign to global variables for public APIs.

-- Named function
function greet(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name
end

print(greet("Lua"))  -- Hello, Lua

-- Local function
local function add(a, b)
    return a + b
end

-- Anonymous function assigned to variable
local multiply = function(a, b)
    return a * b
end

print(add(3, 4))       -- 7
print(multiply(5, 6))  -- 30

-- Function in table
local obj = {
    value = 42,
    getValue = function(self) return self.value end
}
print(obj.getValue(obj))  -- 42
Return Values: Functions can return multiple values using the 'return' keyword with comma-separated expressions. If a function doesn't hit a return statement, it returns nil. Common mistake: capturing multiple returns with a single variable — extra returns are discarded. Best practice: use multiple assignment to capture all return values.

function max_and_min(a, b, c)
    local max = math.max(a, b, c)
    local min = math.min(a, b, c)
    return max, min
end

-- Multiple assignment captures all returns
local mx, mn = max_and_min(10, 3, 7)
print(mx, mn)  -- 10, 3

-- Single variable captures only first return
local mx_only = max_and_min(10, 3, 7)
print(mx_only)  -- 10

-- Discard returns with _
local mx, _ = max_and_min(10, 3, 7)

-- Functions without return return nil
function noop()
    -- no return
end
print(noop())  -- nil
Multiple Returns: Several built-in functions return multiple values: string.find returns start and end positions, pairs returns key and value, ipairs returns index and value. The unpack() function (table.unpack in Lua 5.3+) returns all elements of an array as individual values. Common mistake: wrapping a multi-return function in parentheses discards all but the first value. Best practice: use table.pack() to capture multiple returns in a table.

local s = "hello world"
local start, finish = string.find(s, "world")
print(start, finish)  -- 7, 11

-- unpack() returns all array elements
local t = {10, 20, 30}
print(unpack(t))  -- 10, 20, 30

-- Parentheses discard extra returns
local first = (string.find(s, "world"))
print(first)  -- 7 (only first return)

-- Pack multiple returns into a table
local results = table.pack(string.find(s, "world"))
print(results[1], results[2])  -- 7, 11
print(results.n)  -- 2 (number of elements)
Variadic Args: Variadic functions accept any number of arguments using the ... (three dots) syntax. Use {...} to capture args in a table, or select() to access individual args. Common mistake: using {...} when arguments may contain nil — nil values will be lost in the table. Best practice: use table.pack(...) to capture variadic args including nil values.

function sum(...)
    local total = 0
    for _, v in ipairs({...}) do
        total = total + v
    end
    return total
end

print(sum(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))  -- 15

-- select() to access individual args
function first_and_rest(first, ...)
    return first, {...}
end

local f, rest = first_and_rest("a", "b", "c")
print(f)           -- a
print(#rest)       -- 2

-- select('#', ...) counts variadic args
function count_args(...)
    return select("#", ...)
end
print(count_args(1, 2, 3))  -- 3
Closures and Upvalues: Lua supports lexical scoping: inner functions can access outer function's local variables (upvalues). Each invocation of the outer function creates a new closure with its own upvalues. Common mistake: assuming closures capture values by copy — they capture variables by reference. Best practice: use closures for function factories, callbacks, and iterators.

function make_counter(start)
    local count = start or 0
    return function()
        count = count + 1
        return count
    end
end

local counter1 = make_counter(10)
local counter2 = make_counter(0)

print(counter1())  -- 11
print(counter1())  -- 12
print(counter2())  -- 1
print(counter1())  -- 13

-- Closures for callbacks
local handlers = {}
for i = 1, 3 do
    handlers[i] = function()
        return "Handler " .. i
    end
end
print(handlers[2]())  -- Handler 2
Tail Calls: Lua proper tail calls: when a function ends with return func(args), the current stack frame is reused, preventing stack growth. This enables recursive algorithms without stack overflow. Common mistake: any operation after the call (like return func() + 1) prevents tail call optimization. Best practice: use tail calls for state-machine implementations and recursive algorithms.

-- Proper tail call (stack frame is reused)
function factorial(n, acc)
    acc = acc or 1
    if n <= 1 then return acc end
    return factorial(n - 1, n * acc)  -- tail call
end

print(factorial(5))  -- 120

-- NOT a tail call (addition after call)
function bad_fact(n)
    if n <= 1 then return 1 end
    return n * bad_fact(n - 1)  -- NOT tail
end

-- Tail call syntax: return <function>(<args>)
-- The expression must be exactly 'return func(args)'
-- with no operations on the result
Closures & Upvalues: Lua functions are closures — they capture local variables (upvalues) from their enclosing scope. Each closure instance has its own upvalue set. Closures enable function factories, callbacks, and encapsulation (private state). The upvalues persist even after the outer function returns.

-- Function factory with closure
function makeCounter(start)
    local count = start  -- upvalue
    return function()
        count = count + 1
        return count
    end
end

local c1 = makeCounter(0)
local c2 = makeCounter(100)

print(c1())  -- 1
print(c1())  -- 2
print(c2())  -- 101  (independent upvalue!)
print(c1())  -- 3

-- Private state (encapsulation)
function createAccount(initial)
    local balance = initial  -- upvalue: private!
    return {
        deposit = function(amt)
            balance = balance + amt
        end,
        withdraw = function(amt)
            if amt <= balance then
                balance = balance - amt
                return true
            end
            return false
        end,
        getBalance = function() return balance end
    }
end

local acc = createAccount(100)
acc.deposit(50)
print(acc.getBalance())  -- 150
-- balance is not directly accessible

-- Pitfall: upvalues in loops (capture by reference)
local funcs = {}
for i = 1, 3 do
    funcs[i] = function() return i end
end
print(funcs[1]())  -- 1 (Lua closes the loop variable correctly)

-- Replicate closure state
function makeAdder(x)
    return function(y) return x + y end
end
local add5 = makeAdder(5)
print(add5(3))  -- 8

String Basics: Lua strings are immutable byte sequences. Indexing with # gives byte length, not character count. String positions start at 1 (not 0). Escape sequences in quoted strings: \n (newline), \t (tab), \\ (backslash), \" (double quote), \' (single quote). Common mistake: using string indexing syntax s[i] — Lua doesn't support this; use s:sub(i, i) instead. Best practice: use [[ ]] for multi-line or escape-heavy strings.

local s = "Hello, Lua!"

-- Length (in bytes)
print(#s)  -- 11

-- Substring extraction
print(s:sub(1, 5))   -- "Hello"
print(s:sub(8))      -- "Lua!"
print(s:sub(-4))     -- "Lua!" (negative = from end)

-- Escape sequences
print("Line1\nLine2")     -- newline
print("Tab\there")        -- tab
print("Back\\slash")      -- backslash
print("Quote: \"hi\"")   -- double quote

-- Multi-line with long brackets
print([[Line1
Line2
Line3]])
Concatenation: Use .. for string concatenation. Lua automatically coerces numbers to strings in concatenation context. For large-scale concatenation, use table.concat() which is much more efficient than repeated .. operations. Common mistake: using .. in a loop for building large strings — O(n^2) due to immutable string allocation. Best practice: collect parts in a table and use table.concat() for batch concatenation.

-- Basic concatenation
local greeting = "Hello" .. " " .. "World"
print(greeting)  -- Hello World

-- Number coercion
print("Value: " .. 42)  -- Value: 42

-- INEFFICIENT: repeated concatenation in loop
local function slow_build(n)
    local s = ""
    for i = 1, n do
        s = s .. tostring(i) .. ","
    end
    return s
end

-- EFFICIENT: table.concat
local function fast_build(n)
    local parts = {}
    for i = 1, n do
        parts[#parts + 1] = tostring(i)
        parts[#parts + 1] = ","
    end
    return table.concat(parts)
end

print(fast_build(5))  -- 1,2,3,4,5,
string Library: The string library provides: len(s), sub(s, i, j), upper(s), lower(s), rep(s, n), char(...), and byte(s, i). Methods use colon notation: s:upper(). Common mistake: confusing string.byte (returns numeric codes) with string.char (creates string from codes). Best practice: use colon notation (s:method()) for readability — it passes s as the first argument.

local s = "Lua Programming"

print(string.len(s))          -- 15
print(s:len())                -- 15 (colon notation)
print(s:sub(1, 3))            -- Lua
print(s:upper())              -- LUA PROGRAMMING
print(s:lower())              -- lua programming
print(string.rep("ha", 3))   -- hahaha

-- char and byte (ASCII codes)
print(string.char(65, 66, 67))  -- ABC
print(string.byte("ABC"))       -- 65
print(string.byte("ABC", 2))    -- 66

-- rep for padding
local function pad_left(s, width)
    return string.rep(" ", width - #s) .. s
end
print(pad_left("42", 5))  -- "   42"
string.match: string.match(s, pattern) extracts captures from a string based on a Lua pattern. Returns the first match or nil. Anchored patterns start with ^ (beginning) or end with $ (end). Common mistake: using Lua patterns with regex metacharacters like ? or + — Lua patterns use a different syntax. Best practice: test patterns incrementally, starting simple and adding constraints.

local url = "https://example.com/page?id=42"

-- Extract protocol
local protocol = string.match(url, "^(%a+):")
print(protocol)  -- https

-- Extract domain
local domain = string.match(url, "://([^/]+)")
print(domain)  -- example.com

-- Extract query parameter (single capture)
local id = string.match(url, "id=(%d+)")
print(id)  -- 42

-- Multiple captures
local year, month, day = string.match("2024-01-15", "(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)")
print(year, month, day)  -- 2024 01 15
string.gmatch: string.gmatch(s, pattern) returns an iterator that yields all matches (with or without captures) of a pattern in a string. Use it in for loops or collect all matches into a table. Common mistake: forgetting that gmatch returns captures if the pattern has them, or the full match otherwise. Best practice: use gmatch with captures to extract structured data.

local text = "apple,banana,cherry,date"

-- Iterate over all matches (no captures = full match)
local words = {}
for word in string.gmatch(text, "[^,]+") do
    table.insert(words, word)
end
print(table.concat(words, ", "))  -- apple, banana, cherry, date

-- With captures
local csv = "1,Alice,30\n2,Bob,25\n3,Charlie,35"
for id, name, age in string.gmatch(csv, "(%d+),(%w+),(%d+)") do
    print(name .. " is " .. age .. " years old")
end
string.gsub: string.gsub(s, pattern, replacement) performs global search-and-replace, returning the modified string and a count of replacements. Replacement can be a string, a table (keyed by captures), or a function. Common mistake: forgetting that gsub returns TWO values — the new string and the replacement count. Best practice: use a function replacement for complex transformations.

local s = "hello world, hello lua"

-- Simple string replacement
local result, count = string.gsub(s, "hello", "hi")
print(result)  -- hi world, hi lua
print(count)   -- 2

-- Using captures in replacement string
local s2 = "name=John age=30"
local r2 = string.gsub(s2, "(%w+)=(%w+)", "%1: %2")
print(r2)  -- name: John age: 30

-- Table lookup replacement
local lookup = {hello = "hi", world = "earth"}
local r3 = string.gsub("hello world", "(%w+)", lookup)
print(r3)  -- hi earth

-- Function replacement
local r4 = string.gsub("hello WORLD", "%a+", function(w)
    return w:sub(1, 1):upper() .. w:sub(2):lower()
end)
print(r4)  -- Hello World
Lua Patterns: Lua patterns are simpler than regular expressions. Character classes: %a (letter), %d (digit), %s (whitespace), %w (alphanumeric), . (any). Uppercase means negation: %D = non-digit. Quantifiers: + (one or more), * (zero or more), - (lazy zero or more), ? (zero or one). Captures with (). Common mistake: using regex syntax like \d or [0-9] — use Lua %d or [09] instead. Best practice: use the () (empty capture) to capture positions.

-- Character classes
print(string.match("hello123", "%a+%d*"))  -- hello123

-- Quantifiers: + greedy, - lazy (match minimal)
local s = "<hello><world>"
print(string.match(s, "<.->"))   -- <hello> (lazy)
print(string.match(s, "<.+>"))   -- <hello><world> (greedy)

-- Capture positions with () empty capture
local s2 = "abc123def"
local start, finish = string.match(s2, "%d+()")
print(start, finish)  -- 4, 6 (positions)

-- Frontier pattern %f for word boundaries
local s3 = "cat dog catalog"
for w in string.gmatch(s3, "%f[%a]cat%f[^%a]") do
    print(w)  -- cat (not 'catalog')
end

-- Character sets with []
local hex = string.match("FF", "[0-9A-Fa-f]+")
print(hex)  -- FF

print vs io.write: print() is a simplified output function that adds a tab separator between arguments and a newline at the end. io.write() provides lower-level output with no automatic formatting. Common mistake: using print() when you need exact formatting control — print always adds separators and newlines. Best practice: use print() for quick debugging and io.write() for formatted, precise output.

-- print adds tab separators and newline
print("Hello", "World")  -- Hello\tWorld\n

-- io.write does NOT add newlines
io.write("Hello ")
io.write("World")
io.write("\n")  -- must add newline manually

-- io.write for precise formatting
for i = 1, 3 do
    io.write(tostring(i) .. ": " .. string.rep("*", i) .. "\n")
end

-- Multiple values with io.write
io.write("The answer is ", 42, "\n")
io.read: io.read() reads input from stdin. Formats: '*l' (line, default), '*a' (entire file), '*n' (number), or a number (read that many characters). Returns nil on EOF. Common mistake: io.read('*n') reads a number but stops at whitespace — the newline remains in the buffer. Best practice: use io.read() for line input and tonumber() for numeric conversion.

-- Read a line (default mode '*l')
-- local line = io.read()
-- print("You said: " .. line)

-- Read a number
-- local n = io.read('*n')
-- print("Number: " .. n)

-- Read entire file
-- local content = io.read('*a')

-- Read 10 characters
-- local chunk = io.read(10)

-- Simulating io.read for a script
local data = "42\nhello\n"
-- In a real script, use: local n = io.read('*n')
print("Use io.read('*n') for numbers")
print("Use io.read() for lines")
File I/O: Use io.open(filename, mode) to open files. Modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write, overwrites), 'a' (append), 'r+' (read/write). Returns a file handle or nil + error message. Methods: handle:read(), handle:write(), handle:close(), handle:lines(). Common mistake: forgetting to close files — use a pcall/finally pattern to ensure cleanup. Best practice: use io.lines() for line-by-line reading without manual close.

-- Writing to a file
local f, err = io.open("/tmp/test.txt", "w")
if f then
    f:write("Hello, file!\n")
    f:write("Line 2\n")
    f:close()
    print("File written")
else
    print("Error: " .. err)
end

-- Reading a file
local f, err = io.open("/tmp/test.txt", "r")
if f then
    local content = f:read("*a")  -- read all
    print(content)
    f:close()
end

-- Line-by-line with io.lines (auto-closes)
for line in io.lines("/tmp/test.txt") do
    print("Line: " .. line)
end
Formatted Output: string.format(format, ...) provides C-style printf formatting. Specifiers: %d (integer), %f (float), %s (string), %x (hex), %e (scientific). Width and precision can be specified: %10s (min width 10), %.2f (2 decimal places). Common mistake: using %d for floats or %f for integers — both work but may give unexpected results. Best practice: use specific format specifiers for clarity.

local name = "Lua"
local version = 5.4
local year = 2024

-- Basic formatting
print(string.format("%s version %.1f was released in %d", name, version, year))
-- Lua version 5.4 was released in 2024

-- Width and alignment
print(string.format("|%10s|", "right"))    -- |     right|
print(string.format("|%-10s|", "left"))    -- |left     |

-- Floating point precision
print(string.format("%.3f", math.pi))     -- 3.142
print(string.format("%.10f", math.pi))    -- 3.1415926536

-- Hex and octal
print(string.format("%x %X", 255, 255))   -- ff FF
print(string.format("%o", 255))           -- 377

-- Leading zeros
print(string.format("%04d", 42))          -- 0042
Advanced File Operations: Lua's I/O: io.open(mode) returns file handle or nil+errmsg. Modes: "r" (read), "w" (write), "a" (append), "r+"/"w+"/"a+" (read+write), "b" suffix (binary). Methods: read(format), write, lines, seek, flush, close. read formats: "*a" (all), "*l" (line), "*n" (number), or byte count.

local filename = "data.txt"

-- Write
local f = io.open(filename, "w")
if f then
    f:write("Line 1\n")
    f:write("Line 2\n")
    f:write(string.format("Pi = %.3f\n", math.pi))
    f:close()
end

-- Read all
f = io.open(filename, "r")
if f then
    local content = f:read("*a")  -- read entire file
    print("Content:")
    print(content)
    f:close()
end

-- Read line by line
f = io.open(filename, "r")
if f then
    for line in f:lines() do
        print("Line:", line)
    end
    f:close()
end

-- Seek: set/get file position
f = io.open(filename, "r")
f:seek("set", 6)  -- set position to byte 6
local data = f:read(5)  -- read 5 bytes
print(data)
print("Current pos:", f:seek("cur"))  -- get position
f:close()

-- Append mode
f = io.open(filename, "a")
f:write("Appended line\n")
f:close()

-- Binary mode
f = io.open("binary.dat", "wb")
f:write(string.char(0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE, 0xEF))
f:close()

require: require(name) loads and executes a module, returning the module table. It searches package.path for Lua files and package.cpath for C libraries. Modules are cached in package.loaded — subsequent require calls return the cached version. Common mistake: requiring a module returns the module table but forget to assign it. Best practice: always assign the result of require to a local variable.

-- Basic require
-- local math = require("math")  -- math is built-in, no need

-- Require a custom module
-- local mylib = require("mylib")

-- Package.path shows search locations
print(package.path)

-- Module caching (second call returns cached)
local m1 = require("math")  -- or any other module
local m2 = require("math")  -- returns cached version
print(m1 == m2)  -- true

-- Check if a module is loaded
print(package.loaded["math"])  -- table (module exists)

-- Remove from cache to force reload
-- package.loaded["mymodule"] = nil
-- mymodule = require("mymodule")  -- fresh load
Module Pattern: The standard Lua module pattern: create a local table, add functions to it, and return it at the end. Use local variables for private/internal functions. Common mistake: polluting the global namespace — module internals should be local. Best practice: follow the standard pattern of returning a table with only public functions.

-- mymodule.lua would contain:
-- local mymodule = {}
-- 
-- local function private_helper()
--     return "internal"
-- end
-- 
-- function mymodule.greet(name)
--     return "Hello, " .. name
-- end
-- 
-- function mymodule.add(a, b)
--     return a + b
-- end
-- 
-- return mymodule

-- Usage (simulated inline):
local mymodule = {}

local function private_helper()
    return "internal"
end

function mymodule.greet(name)
    return "Hello, " .. name
end

function mymodule.add(a, b)
    return a + b
end

-- Only public interface exposed
print(mymodule.greet("Lua"))  -- Hello, Lua
print(mymodule.add(3, 4))      -- 7
package.path: package.path controls where Lua looks for Lua modules. The default path uses ?.lua and ?/init.lua patterns. LUA_PATH environment variable overrides it. You can manipulate package.path at runtime to add search paths. Common mistake: module files not found because they're not in package.path — always check the search path. Best practice: use the LUA_PATH environment variable or add paths programmatically.

-- Default search paths
print("Default search path:")
print(package.path)

-- Add a custom path (at the beginning)
package.path = "./mylibs/?.lua;" .. package.path

-- Using ? placeholder
-- If require("utils") is called with path "./libs/?.lua",
-- Lua searches for ./libs/utils.lua

-- Check where Lua will look for a module
local function find_module(name)
    for path in string.gmatch(package.path, "[^;]+") do
        local full = string.gsub(path, "%?", name)
        local f = io.open(full, "r")
        if f then
            f:close()
            return full
        end
    end
    return nil
end

print(find_module("math"))
Module Best Practices: Lua modules should return a table, use local variables for private members, and avoid polluting the global namespace. Use 'local' by default. Name modules in lowercase with underscores. Place modules in a clear directory structure. Common mistake: defining module functions as globals — this pollutes the global namespace and can cause conflicts. Best practice: encapsulate all module code in a local table and return it.

-- GOOD module pattern:
-- local mylib = {}
-- 
-- local function private()
--     return "secret"
-- end
-- 
-- function mylib.public_func()
--     return private()
-- end
-- 
-- return mylib

-- BAD: global pollution
-- function bad_global() end  -- DON'T

-- Module naming conventions
-- Use: mymodule, string_utils, http_client
-- NOT: MyModule, string-utils, HTTPClient

-- Environment safety: use _ENV instead of globals
local mylib = {}

function mylib.safe_greet()
    return "Hello"
end

return mylib

Metatables: Metatables control table behavior through metamethods (events). setmetatable(t, mt) assigns a metatable to table t; getmetatable(t) retrieves it. Metamethods are triggered by operations like indexing, arithmetic, and comparison. Common mistake: trying to set metatables on non-table types (numbers, strings) — only tables and userdata can have metatables in standard Lua. Best practice: use metatables sparingly for domain-specific behaviors.

local t = {}
local mt = {
    __tostring = function()
        return "[custom table]"
    end
}
setmetatable(t, mt)

print(t)  -- [custom table]

-- Metatables are themselves tables
print(getmetatable(t))  -- table: 0x...

-- Multiple metatables can share behavior
local t2 = {}
setmetatable(t2, mt)

-- Tables can be their own metatable (advanced)
-- setmetatable(t, t)  -- self-referencing
__index: __index is the most commonly used metamethod. It provides fallback behavior when a key doesn't exist in a table. It can be a table (lookup in that table) or a function (called with table and key). Common mistake: confusing __index with __newindex — __index handles MISSING key reads; __newindex handles MISSING key writes. Best practice: use __index with a table for simple inheritance and with a function for computed lookups.

-- __index as a table (prototype inheritance)
local animal = {
    sound = "?",
    speak = function(self)
        return self.sound
    end
}

local dog = {sound = "Woof!"}
setmetatable(dog, {__index = animal})

print(dog.speak(dog))    -- Woof! (found in dog)
print(dog.sound)          -- Woof!

-- Inheriting a method not in child
local cat = {}
setmetatable(cat, {__index = animal})
cat.sound = "Meow!"
print(cat:speak())        -- Meow! (colon syntax)

-- __index as a function
local defaults = setmetatable({}, {
    __index = function(_, key)
        return "default_" .. key
    end
})
print(defaults["name"])   -- default_name
__newindex: __newindex intercepts assignments to keys that don't exist in the table. It can be a table (writes go to that table) or a function (receives table, key, value). Common mistake: __newindex doesn't prevent writes to EXISTING keys — it only fires for MISSING keys. Best practice: combine __index and __newindex for controlled table access patterns.

-- __newindex as a function
local monitored = {}
local mt = {
    __newindex = function(t, key, value)
        print("Setting " .. tostring(key) .. " = " .. tostring(value))
        rawset(t, key, value)  -- must use rawset!
    end
}
setmetatable(monitored, mt)

monitored.name = "Lua"  -- prints: Setting name = Lua
print(monitored.name)    -- Lua

-- Read-only table pattern
local function readonly(t)
    local proxy = {}
    setmetatable(proxy, {
        __index = t,
        __newindex = function()
            error("Table is read-only")
        end
    })
    return proxy
end

local original = {x = 10}
local ro = readonly(original)
print(ro.x)     -- 10
-- ro.x = 20    -- ERROR: Table is read-only
__call: The __call metamethod makes a table callable as a function. The metamethod receives the table as the first argument, followed by any call arguments. Common mistake: forgetting that the table itself is passed as the first argument to __call. Best practice: use __call for function objects (functors) that maintain state.

local function create_counter(start)
    local counter = {count = start or 0}
    setmetatable(counter, {
        __call = function(self, increment)
            increment = increment or 1
            self.count = self.count + increment
            return self.count
        end
    })
    return counter
end

local c = create_counter(10)
print(c())     -- 11
print(c(5))    -- 16
print(c())     -- 17

-- Constructor pattern with __call
local Person = {}
Person.__index = Person

function Person:new(name, age)
    return setmetatable({name = name, age = age}, Person)
end

function Person:greet()
    return "Hi, I'm " .. self.name
end

local p = Person:new("Alice", 30)
print(p:greet())  -- Hi, I'm Alice
Arithmetic Metamethods: Lua supports arithmetic metamethods: __add, __sub, __mul, __div, __mod, __pow, __unm (unary minus), __concat, and __tostring. These enable operator overloading on tables. Common mistake: forgetting to handle both operand orders — __add only fires when the first operand has the metatable. Best practice: define all relevant metamethods for consistent behavior.
OOP via Prototypes: Lua implements object-oriented programming through prototype-based inheritance using metatables. The colon syntax (obj:method()) is syntactic sugar for (obj.method(obj)) — it automatically passes the object as 'self'. Common mistake: forgetting 'self' parameter or colon syntax when calling methods. Best practice: always use colon syntax for method definitions (:method) and method calls (:method()).

-- Define a class table
local Animal = {}
Animal.__index = Animal

-- Constructor
function Animal:new(name, sound)
    local obj = {name = name, sound = sound}
    setmetatable(obj, Animal)
    return obj
end

-- Method (colon syntax)
function Animal:speak()
    return self.name .. " says " .. self.sound
end

-- Subclass "inheritance"
local Dog = {}
setmetatable(Dog, {__index = Animal})
Dog.__index = Dog

function Dog:new(name)

coroutine.create/resume/yield: Coroutines allow cooperative multitasking: a coroutine can yield (pause) execution and be resumed later from where it left off. coroutine.create(f) creates a coroutine. coroutine.resume(co, ...) starts or resumes it. coroutine.yield(...) suspends execution and returns values to the resumer. Common mistake: trying to resume a dead (finished) coroutine — it will return false + error message. Best practice: check the first return value of resume (true = success, false = error).

local function my_task()
    print("Task: start")
    coroutine.yield("yielded value")  -- pause here
    print("Task: resumed")
    return "done"
end

local co = coroutine.create(my_task)

-- First resume
local ok, result = coroutine.resume(co)
print(ok, result)  -- true, yielded value

-- Second resume
local ok, result = coroutine.resume(co)
print(ok, result)  -- true, done

-- Attempting to resume dead coroutine
local ok, err = coroutine.resume(co)
print(ok, err)  -- false, cannot resume dead coroutine
coroutine.status: coroutine.status(co) returns the state: 'suspended' (created or just yielded), 'running' (currently executing), 'dead' (finished or errored), or 'normal' (resumed another coroutine). Common mistake: calling status from within the running coroutine — it returns 'running'. Best practice: use status() to check if a coroutine can be resumed before calling resume.

local co = coroutine.create(function()
    print("Inside: " .. coroutine.status(co))  -- running
    coroutine.yield()
    print("Back inside")
end)

print(coroutine.status(co))  -- suspended
coroutine.resume(co)
print(coroutine.status(co))  -- suspended (just yielded)
coroutine.resume(co)
print(coroutine.status(co))  -- dead

-- Safe resume
if coroutine.status(co) == "suspended" then
    coroutine.resume(co)
else
    print("Coroutine cannot be resumed")
end
coroutine.wrap: coroutine.wrap(f) creates a coroutine and returns a function that resumes it. Unlike coroutine.resume, errors are propagated as exceptions instead of returning false. Common mistake: wrap returns a function that throws errors — use pcall around it for error handling. Best practice: use wrap for simple iterator-like coroutines where you don't need error handling per step.

local function task()
    for i = 1, 3 do
        coroutine.yield(i * 10)
    end
    return "finished"
end

local wrapped = coroutine.wrap(task)

print(wrapped())  -- 10
print(wrapped())  -- 20
print(wrapped())  -- 30
print(wrapped())  -- finished

-- Error handling with wrap
local function faulty()
    error("something went wrong")
end

local wrapped_faulty = coroutine.wrap(faulty)
local ok, err = pcall(wrapped_faulty)
print(ok, err)  -- false, something went wrong
Producer-Consumer Example: Coroutines excel at the producer-consumer pattern: a producer yields values as they become available, and a consumer resumes the producer to get the next value. Common mistake: not handling the end-of-production condition properly. Best practice: use a sentinel value (like nil) to signal end of production.

-- Producer: generates values on demand
function producer(max)
    return coroutine.wrap(function()
        for i = 1, max do
            coroutine.yield(i)
        end
        return nil  -- end of production
    end)
end

-- Consumer: processes values
local gen = producer(5)
local val = gen()
while val do
    print("Consumed: " .. val)
    val = gen()
end

-- Filter pattern with coroutines
function filter(gen, predicate)
    return coroutine.wrap(function()
        for v in gen do
            if predicate(v) then
                coroutine.yield(v)
            end
        end
    end)
end

-- Pipeline
local numbers = producer(10)
local evens = filter(numbers, function(n) return n % 2 == 0 end)
for v in evens do
    print("Even: " .. v)
end
Coroutine Use Cases: Coroutines are useful for: generators (lazy sequences), cooperative multitasking (game loops), state machines (each state is a yield point), and asynchronous I/O simulation. Common mistake: using coroutines for CPU-bound parallelism — Lua's coroutines are cooperative, not preemptive; they don't use multiple cores. Best practice: use coroutines for I/O-bound or event-driven programming.

-- Generator: infinite sequence
function fib_gen()
    return coroutine.wrap(function()
        local a, b = 0, 1
        while true do
            coroutine.yield(a)
            a, b = b, a + b
        end
    end)
end

local fib = fib_gen()
for i = 1, 10 do
    print(fib())
end

-- State machine as coroutine
function traffic_light()
    while true do
        print("GREEN")
        coroutine.yield(30)
        print("YELLOW")
        coroutine.yield(3)
        print("RED")
        coroutine.yield(20)
    end
end

local light = coroutine.wrap(traffic_light)
light()  -- GREEN, returns 30
light()  -- YELLOW, returns 3
light()  -- RED, returns 20

pcall: pcall(f, ...) calls function f in protected mode (like try-catch). Returns true + results on success, or false + error message on failure. pcall catches all errors and prevents them from propagating. Common mistake: not checking the first return value of pcall — always check if the call succeeded. Best practice: use pcall for operations that might fail with expected error types.

local function divide(a, b)
    if b == 0 then
        error("division by zero")
    end
    return a / b
end

-- Successful call
local ok, result = pcall(divide, 10, 2)
if ok then
    print(result)  -- 5
end

-- Failed call (no crash)
local ok, err = pcall(divide, 10, 0)
if not ok then
    print("Error: " .. err)  -- Error: division by zero
end

-- pcall with multiple returns
local function stats(t)
    if #t == 0 then error("empty table") end
    local sum = 0
    for _, v in ipairs(t) do sum = sum + v end
    return sum, sum / #t
end

local ok, sum, avg = pcall(stats, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5})
if ok then
    print(sum, avg)  -- 15, 3
end
xpcall: xpcall(f, err_handler, ...) is like pcall but with a custom error handler function. The handler receives the error message and can augment it with debug information. Common mistake: forgetting that the error handler runs in protected mode too — errors in the handler are caught. Best practice: use xpcall with debug.traceback to get detailed stack traces.

local function divide(a, b)
    if b == 0 then
        error("division by zero")
    end
    return a / b
end

-- Error handler that adds stack trace
local function my_error_handler(err)
    print("Custom handler called")
    return "HANDLED: " .. err .. "\n" .. debug.traceback()
end

-- Using xpcall
local ok, result = xpcall(function()
    return divide(10, 0)
end, my_error_handler)

if not ok then
    print(result)  -- Includes custom handler message + traceback
end

-- xpcall with anonymous error handler
pcall(function()
    error("direct error")
end)

-- debug.traceback in xpcall
xpcall(function()
    error("test")
end, function(err)
    return debug.traceback(err, 2)
end)
error: error(message, level) raises an error that terminates the current function unless caught by pcall/xpcall. The level parameter (1 = caller of error, 2 = caller's caller, etc.) controls where the error traceback points. Common mistake: not providing helpful error messages — good error messages include expected and actual values. Best practice: use descriptive error messages that help diagnose the problem.

function check_positive(n)
    if type(n) ~= "number" then
        error("expected number, got " .. type(n), 2)
    end
    if n <= 0 then
        error("value must be positive, got " .. n, 2)
    end
    return math.sqrt(n)
end

-- Level 2 error points to the caller's location
function wrapper(x)
    return check_positive(x)
end

-- Error messages can be any type (table, etc.)
function validate(config)
    if not config.name then
        error({code = "MISSING_NAME", msg = "name required"})
    end
end

-- Catching table errors
local ok, err = pcall(validate, {})
if not ok and type(err) == "table" then
    print(err.code, err.msg)  -- MISSING_NAME, name required
end
assert: assert(condition, message) combines assertion and error handling. If condition is truthy, returns it. If falsy, raises an error with the message (default: 'assertion failed!'). Common mistake: using assert for validation in production code — assert can be stripped in some contexts. Best practice: use assert for input validation and preconditions, not for runtime error handling.

local function open_file(filename)
    local f, err = io.open(filename, "r")
    assert(f, "Failed to open " .. filename .. ": " .. (err or "unknown error"))
    return f
end

-- Successful
local f = assert(io.open("/tmp/test.txt", "w"))
f:close()

-- Failed (if file doesn't exist)
-- local f = assert(io.open("/nonexistent/file.txt", "r"))
-- Error: /nonexistent/file.txt: No such file or directory

-- assert returns the condition value
local function ensure(condition, msg)
    return assert(condition, msg or "assertion failed")
end

-- Idiomatic assert for table fields
local config = {port = 8080}
local port = assert(config.port, "config.port is required")
print("Port: " .. port)

math: The math library provides standard mathematical functions. Key functions: math.abs, math.max/min, math.floor/ceil, math.random, math.sin/cos/tan, math.sqrt, math.log. Constants: math.pi, math.huge (infinity). math.randomseed() seeds the random generator. Common mistake: forgetting to call math.randomseed() before using math.random() — you'll get the same sequence every run. Best practice: use math.randomseed(os.time()) for different sequences per run.

print(math.pi)         -- 3.1415926535898
print(math.huge)        -- inf
print(math.abs(-10))    -- 10
print(math.max(3, 7, 2)) -- 7
print(math.floor(3.7))  -- 3

math.randomseed(os.time())

table (full recap): The table library provides essential table manipulation functions. Key functions: table.insert, table.remove, table.sort, table.concat, table.unpack (Lua 5.3+), and table.move (Lua 5.3+). table.unpack returns all elements of an array as separate values. table.move copies elements within or between tables. Common mistake: table.sort is unstable — equal elements may not preserve their original order. Best practice: combine table.sort with a comparison function for complex sorting.

local t = {3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6}

-- Sort with custom comparator
table.sort(t, function(a, b) return a > b end)
print(table.concat(t, ", "))  -- 9, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1

-- table.unpack (Lua 5.3+)
local args = {10, 20, 30}
local max = math.max(table.unpack(args))
print(max)  -- 30

-- table.move (Lua 5.3+)
local src = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
local dst = {}
table.move(src, 1, 3, 1, dst)  -- copy src[1..3] to dst[1..]
print(table.concat(dst, ", "))  -- 1, 2, 3

-- table.pack (Lua 5.3+)
local packed = table.pack("a", "b", nil, "c")
print(packed.n)  -- 4 (includes nil slots)

All operations work on 32-bit unsigned integers. Common mistake: using bitwise operators (&, |, ^) that don't exist in Lua — use the bit32 library functions. Best practice: use bit32 for flags, permissions, and low-level data manipulation.

local a, b = 0b1010, 0b1100  -- binary literals (Lua 5.3+)

print(bit32.band(a, b))  -- 8  (0b1000)
print(bit32.bor(a, b))   -- 14 (0b1110)
print(bit32.bxor(a, b))  -- 6  (0b0110)
print(bit32.bnot(a))     -- -11 (0xfffffff5)

-- Shifts
print(bit32.lshift(1, 3))  -- 8  (1 << 3)
print(bit32.rshift(8, 2))  -- 2  (8 >> 2)

-- Bit extraction
local flags = 0b10110100
print(bit32.extract(flags, 2, 4))  -- 0b1101 (bits 2-5)

-- Bit replacement
print(bit32.replace(flags, 0b1001, 0, 4))  -- 0b10011001

Weak Tables: Weak tables allow the garbage collector to reclaim objects even though they're referenced in the table. Modes: __mode = 'k' (weak keys), 'v' (weak values), or 'kv' (both). Used for memoization, object associations, and caching without preventing GC. Common mistake: using weak tables with non-collectible keys (numbers, booleans) — they don't support weak references. Best practice: use weak-value tables for caches and weak-key tables for object properties.

-- Weak values: cached values can be GC'd
local cache = setmetatable({}, {__mode = "v"})

function compute_expensive(key)
    local result = cache[key]
    if result then
        print("Cache hit: " .. key)
        return result
    end
    result = key .. "_computed"
    cache[key] = result
    return result
end

print(compute_expensive("a"))  -- computed
print(compute_expensive("a"))  -- cache hit

-- Weak keys: associate data with objects
local metadata = setmetatable({}, {__mode = "k"})

local obj = {name = "test"}
metadata[obj] = {created = os.time()}

print(metadata[obj].created)  -- timestamp
obj = nil  -- object can be GC'd now

-- Weak table with both
local wkt = setmetatable({}, {__mode = "kv"})
Garbage Collection: Lua uses incremental garbage collection. collectgarbage(opt) controls the collector: collectgarbage('collect') forces a full cycle, collectgarbage('count') reports memory in KB, collectgarbage('stop') pauses the collector. Lua 5.4 introduced generational mode. Common mistake: assuming collectgarbage('count') returns bytes — it returns kilobytes. Best practice: let the GC run automatically; only intervene for latency-sensitive code.

-- Force garbage collection
collectgarbage("collect")

-- Memory usage (in KB)
local mem_before = collectgarbage("count")

local big_table = {}
for i = 1, 100000 do
    big_table[i] = {}
end

local mem_after = collectgarbage("count")
print("Memory delta: " .. (mem_after - mem_before) .. " KB")

-- Stop and restart GC
collectgarbage("stop")  -- pause collector for latency
-- ... latency-critical code ...
collectgarbage("restart")

-- Lua 5.4: generational mode (faster, less memory-sensitive)
-- collectgarbage("generational", 0, 0)

-- Step GC
-- collectgarbage("step", 100)  -- do 100 KB of GC work

-- Total memory
print("Total memory: " .. collectgarbage("count") .. " KB")
Environment (_ENV): Lua 5.2+ uses _ENV to control the environment of a chunk. _ENV is a table that stores global variables. Changing _ENV enables sandboxing and module isolation. Common mistake: assuming _ENV affects the entire Lua state — it only affects the current chunk/function. Best practice: use _ENV for creating restricted execution environments and sandboxes.

-- Default environment contains standard globals
print(_ENV)  -- table containing print, math, etc.

-- Create a sandbox with restricted globals
local sandbox_env = {
    print = print,
    math = {max = math.max, min = math.min},
    string = {upper = string.upper},
}

local function run_sandboxed(code)
    local f = load(code, "sandbox", "t", sandbox_env)
    if f then
        return pcall(f)
    else
        return false, "Failed to compile"
    end
end

-- This works
local ok, result = run_sandboxed("return math.max(10, 20)")
print(result)  -- 20

-- This fails (no io in sandbox)
local ok, err = run_sandboxed("return io.open('/etc/passwd')")
print(ok, err)  -- false, attempt to index a nil value (io)

-- Module-level _ENV
-- At top of module: _ENV = {}  -- isolate module globals
Debug Library: The debug library provides introspection capabilities. debug.getinfo(f) returns a table with function metadata. debug.getlocal(f, i) and debug.getupvalue(f, i) inspect local/upvalue variables. debug.traceback() returns a stack trace string. debug.sethook sets function hooks for profiling. Common mistake: using debug library in production code — it's designed for debugging and development. Best practice: restrict debug library usage to development tools and testing.

function example(a, b)
    local c = a + b
    -- Introspect current function
    local info = debug.getinfo(1, "nS")
    print("Function: " .. info.name)
    print("Defined at: " .. info.source .. ":" .. info.linedefined)
    
    -- List local variables
    local i = 1
    while true do
        local name, value = debug.getlocal(1, i)
        if not name then break end
        print("Local " .. name .. " = " .. tostring(value))
        i = i + 1
    end
    
    return c
end

print(example(3, 4))

-- Stack trace
function inner()
    print(debug.traceback())
end

function outer()
    inner()
end

outer()
